source.title: Revisiting Early-Learning Regularization When Federated Learning Meets Noisy Labels
source.authors: Taehyeon Kim; Donggyu Kim; SeYoung Yun

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendix are present; no obvious truncation or garbling affects the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: Tests noisy-label memorization in federated learning, an extension of the claim to a federated setting. It does not test completely random labels in the original centralized settings.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own results on memorization under synthetic and real-world label noise. The cited random-label and early-learning findings in Related Work are not this study's results. Rows below capture the directly relevant CIFAR-10 vanilla FedAvg results in Table 1; the paper's other method-comparison results do not directly measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures noisy-label memorization and early-learning dynamics in federated ResNet training. Its vanilla FedAvg experiments bear on V4 and V6 in a new setting, although they do not test completely random labeling of the entire dataset.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors identify local and global noisy-label memorization in federated learning and conclude that FLR mitigates both while improving global-model accuracy across i.i.d. and non-i.i.d. settings. They acknowledge that it may not suit every type of label noise.
record.recipe_differences: Federated learning with clients, FedAvg aggregation, and synthetic or real-world label noise; the paper studies noisy-label memorization and a federated regularizer rather than random-label fitting in centralized networks.
record.method_sensitivity: Data heterogeneity and whether measurements are made server-side or client-side correspond to different memorization outcomes in Table 1.
record.problems: The directly relevant baseline results are for CIFAR-10 in federated settings. Table 1 reports one last-round measurement per setting without uncertainty. Figure 2 provides described trends but no extractable numeric values in the supplied text. The paper does not measure training error on the full training set or test error at chance.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows selected: other tables and figures primarily report FLR or alternative-method performance, rather than a direct measure of the claim's specified behavior. Figure 2's qualitative baseline trends are recorded in the V6 verdict, not as numeric rows.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling of the entire training set, near-zero training error with chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters relative to true-label training.
Relative time required to fit true versus random labels and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
A controlled sweep from zero to complete label randomization demonstrating both perfect training fit and steadily increasing test error toward chance.
The effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization. FLR is a different regularizer.
Learning dynamics under completely random labeling and whether the same ordering holds across other architectures and noise settings.

missing.what: Qualitative trajectory rows for vanilla FedAvg: early ground-truth learning followed by increasing noisy-label memorization server-side, and rapid local memorization eventually reaching 100%. The record acknowledges these curves but needs rows to support its V6 verdict.

Vanilla clean-label training accuracies accompanying the memorization rows: global/local 69.10%/95.38% in the non-i.i.d. setting and 90.92%/99.96% in the i.i.d. setting. These distinguish full training fit from fitting only the noisy subset.
missing.locator: Table 1, Vanilla rows, clean-label Correct columns

record.verdict_notes: The noise parameters describe the fraction of noisy clients and a lower bound on client corruption rates; neither reported setting randomizes every training label. The two Table 1 settings change both noise configuration and heterogeneity, so their differences do not isolate either factor. FLR's mitigation results do not challenge V5, which names different regularizers.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labeling, zero or near-zero training error, test error at chance, and unchanged original architecture and training hyperparameters.
Training time for fitting random versus true labels, and convergence as corruption increases.
The study does not establish perfect training fit at every noise level, or a steadily rising test error toward chance across none-to-all corruption.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation stop random-label fitting, or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
The paper describes clean-label and noisy-label behavior over training, but reports the relevant Figure 2 curves without extractable numeric values; its own text describes the trends.
